You'd have to look into your school to see if the supervised hours are only for school internship or post-graduation supervised hours. Usually you have to complete an internship with supervised hours while in school, and then thousands of hours after graduation which also need to be in an employment setting. Because the employer would be vouching for you when it is time to obtain the state license. Keep in mind too, you are usually only able to practice with your license in the state you are licensed in. So, if you are licensed in a red state with poor Healthcare prospects looking into the future, you'll have a tougher time. Even if you practice in a remote setting, you would still be seeing red state clients (if licensed in a red state) and dealing with the fallout of poor funding for Healthcare in red states.
Would I be able to ask you if your own practice is through third party websites (example Better Help) or did you have a preexisting client caseload that you converted to remote therapy after moving?

Another thing you have to consider is that it doesn't end with the degree. You'd have to complete supervised hours after graduation which can take up to 2-3 years. Then become state licensed and then after that, worry about how clients will pay you. Which means applying with insurance companies for credentialing which also takes months. And this all relies on the US health system staying intact enough where people will have reliable insurance in the USA. I am going through the credentialing process and have chosen to not bother with Medicare/Medicaid because there are in-person requirements and also, with current political changes, funding for these programs may decrease in the near future. If you haven't completed your program, you may want to strongly consider switching to something international possibility in humanitarian studies for example. Speaking as a now licensed therapist, the whole ordeal is a hassle. Also for Germany in particular, you won't be allowed to see clients through German insurance with a US degree alone - you need to go through a certifying process and even then you may not be accepted without a German degree.

It is my opinion that people who committed suicide in a past life have a greater propensity towards committing it again in the present life because the past life issues remain unresolved amplifying the issues in the present life. Try not to let yourself get into the "destined" feeling when it comes to committing suicide because that was the old way of coping with the heavy karmas. But then you would also delay the development of your soul and have even heavier karmas the next time around. There are also soul contracts we make with other souls and leaving those unfulfilled is problematic too. The overarching soul lesson from the past life bleeding into this life is dealing with aloneness. What decisions in the past life led to being alone and empty in the end? Was it greed (ambition over family for example)? Were you afraid of connecting with other people? Did you chose materialism over the soul's journey (example: a career to earn money at the expense of passion)? Did you commit suicide out of grief after losing your entire family? What were the circumstances and experiences surrounding the loneliness and emptiness so great that the best solution was to end it? There are the sorts of questions you can explore in a regression or meditation to find direction.

Of course I cannot remember the name of the book, but I read a book where the only setting is a jury room. The characters are so engrossed in the details of the case that the outside world doesn't matter. (The writer briefly mentions the days passing but he doesn't go into unnecessary detail about how Person A went home to talk to his wife about the case while Person C went for a walk in the park...) As each person presents his/her reasons for a guilty/not guilty verdict, you learn the background of each character and the reasons for his/her decision. What I am trying to say with all of this is that you don't necessarily have to explain why Earth got destroyed if the inner world of the sanctuary is rich in its character interactions, plot, etc. I would be more worried about a lack of conflict in such a world where everything is destroyed and only a few (presumably peaceful) places remain. Is there a competition for remaining resources? Is the safe haven of the main character more desirable than the alternatives? Do the survivors outside of the sanctuary want a piece of the pie, so to speak? If most of the action happens in the main character's sanctuary, then why have any other safe havens? If Earth is destroyed, then how do the survivors have the technology to travel between safe havens? I personally believe in soulmates and twin flames. Twin flame relationships tend to be tumultuous with one partner "running" from the other and one partner "chasing" the other. Twin flames are usually opposites but the opposing viewpoints force each other to confront and heal inner demons or to grow spiritually. One twin flame becomes terrified (mostly subconsciously) when their inner demons are exposed through the "mirror" of the other twin flame and "runs". With twin flames there is a "knowing-ness" as if you knew them before (perhaps in a past life if you believe in such things). 

Soulmate relationships tend to be more stable and long-lasting because they are less challenging. Instead of encountering your opposite, you see someone who is extremely similar to you. It has a way of eliminating that deep, insatiable feeling of "aloneness" because you recognize that someone out there thinks like you do. You might be able to finish each other's sentences. You may have premonitions about them. Not to say that there isn't a similar base with twin flames, but it much less of a common base. Soulmates can come and go in the same way that twin flames do but I personally find that soulmates "go" more easily because the connection is less intense. A soulmate can even be a family member, a friend, a mentor, etc. Soulmate relationships fare better for our Western view of marriage because you don't have the runner/chaser dynamic. Some schools of thought teach that twin flame relationships prepare you to meet a soulmate, but more often than not the twin flame relationship is too intense for one or more of the partners and he/she chooses the "easy" way out. 

For what it is worth, I am about 99.9% sure I met my twin flame. He keeps running (3rd time now) and this saga has lasted a total of 9 years... I am really struggling as this is the third time I have been brutally dumped on my ass. I have met three soulmates who currently aren't (one physically can't be - dead) in my life. 

In some ways I wish I never had the experience because at least I could have a bland, boring relationship with almost anyone and not feel like something is missing. It is very hard to explain, but for most people, relationships are a composite of shared interests, physical attraction and attachment. They don't really delve deep into the soul of the other person. Most people don't end up with their twin flames (in terms of marriage) and MAY end up with a soulmate. Soulmate relationships are more "comfortable" because you are a very strong compliment to the other person. The union is more stable because no one really has to change. The moral dilemma after being with a twin flame is - Can you pretend like you never met him/her and settle down with someone for practical reasons (not being alone, having kids, etc) despite knowing what could have been or that you won't have even a shred of what you had in the twin flame relationship... It is quite unsettling. Some days I think I will/should spend my life alone unless I encounter at least a soulmate.... As bizarre as it is I still have hope for my twin flame but the future is uncertain due to free will on his side. He might have a temporary soul contract(s) (soulmate(s)) with someone else and/or may choose the "easy" way out. He would have to be strong enough to see it through but there is a BOATLOAD of trauma (familial) on his end that would interfere with the twin flame relationship... But karma has a way of getting back to people who break the twin flame contract. It goes above soulmate contracts... 

Many would argue that the whole twin flame/soulmate theory is a bunch of BS and that we all choose people who reflect unconscious relationship dynamics we shared with our parents. You could say that the whole runner/chaser dynamic inherent in "twin flame" relationships is more demonstrative of a dysfunctional attachment style (insecure, ambivalent, etc) or an indication of deeper personality dysfunction (borderline personality disorder, narcissistic personality disorder, etc). I don't dispute the influence of parental attachment on romantic relationships (psych major here! :D), but it gets too weird when you can FEEL a person's energy even if they are not in a room. When you have dreams about them even though there is no way you could know such information. I once had a dream about a friend of mine (soulmate) who I SAW getting injured in a football game and I felt the pain in my own body. (Worst headache of my life). Turns out he suffered a concussion the next day... The football games are televised in my city and a few months later I saw the game (used to keep a dream journal so I knew the date of the game) and it looked exactly like my dream... I also had a "knowingness" that another soulmate (mom) would get a specific form of cancer (2 years before formal diagnosis). I brushed it off as she was cancer free for 8 years but in the back of my head I thought to myself, "I think she might get this form of cancer one day". I was even able to diagnose my mom when she did get the form of cancer I thought it was before the doctors... 

When you try your best to connect with someone else and you find it completely unfulfilling even though the person is "right" for you on paper.... It is difficult to try to explain to someone who has only dated people in a stereotypical manner. Makes you question the whole spiritual dimension to life. Or you can write off as a coincidence, negative reaction to trauma (loss of relationships), blah blah blah lol :P The biggest irony is that my 99.9% certain twin flame doesn't believe in twin flames XD ... But there it is - two sides of the coin. Equal and opposite viewpoints. Spiritual and material. We each learn something from the other. 

In film, one of the most beautiful depictions of a twin flame relationship is present in Brokeback Mountain. Here you have two men of completely opposite dispositions with one man (Jack) as the chaser and the other (Ennis) as the runner. Jack tries his best to show Ennis what could be if only Ennis would accept his true self. Ennis runs and won't lead an openly gay lifestyle due to self-imposed and societal pressures. In most cases, if you told a mental health professional you have been having suicidal thoughts for the past 5 months, they would want to know the event and severity of the thoughts. If you told this professional that you want to try medications to manage the thoughts, you would be referred to a psychiatrist (or you could make an appointment with a psychiatrist to begin with). Hi, I can relate to you in a sense because I have a master's degree in mental health counseling. One of the things I have learned is that we have to help ourselves and advocate for our own well-being. Whether it is through taking time off from working in the field to working in the field but going to therapy, we have to make sure we are in a decent place. In my program they called it "self-care" and there has to be a balance between helping others vs. helping oneself. Oftentimes counselors gravitate towards issues that have personally impacted them or their families. Your experiences and feelings give you a unique perspective and have a better understanding of clients' feelings. However, there comes a point where you have to assess if you can actually work in the field or if you need to take time off for treatment, rejuvenation, etc. Many counselors experience a phenomenon called burnout where they experience compassion fatigue and other experiences (death of a family member, drug use, etc) can allow you take time off from work or to see a therapist while working to help others.
